content.text:
1. Predict first: does a 5-digit lock have about 50 passwords, about 1000, or many more?
2. Solve a simpler lock first: 2 digits give 10 choices for each of 10 choices, so 100.
3. Each new slot multiplies by 10: 3 digits give 1000, listed 000, 001, and so on up to 999.
4. 5 digits give 10 to the power 5, which is 1 lakh passwords, from 00000 to 99999.

content.text:
Worked example: How many passwords does a 2-digit, a 3-digit and a 5-digit lock have?
1. 2 digits: 10 choices for the first slot, and 10 for the second for each of them: 10 × 10 = 100.
2. 3 digits: each of the 100 passwords takes 10 third digits: 100 × 10 = 1000.
3. 4 digits: 1000 × 10 = 10000. 5 digits: 10000 × 10 = 100000.
4. That is 10 to the power 5 passwords, from 00000 to 99999.
Answer: 100, 1000 and 100000 passwords

concepts.concept_name: Letter locks and codes around us

content.text:
Estu says, "Next time, I will buy a lock that has 6 slots with the letters A to Z. I feel it is safer." How many passwords are possible with such a lock?
Think about how many combinations are possible in different contexts. Some examples are: (i) Pincodes of places in India. The Pincode of Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh is 464001. The Pincode of Zemabawk in Mizoram is 796017. (ii) Mobile numbers. (iii) Vehicle registration numbers.
Try to find out how these numbers or codes are allotted or generated.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is a 6-letter lock safer than a 5-digit lock?
2. Each slot now has 26 choices, so 6 slots give 26 multiplied by itself 6 times.
3. 26 to the power 6 is 308915776, more than 3000 times the 100000 passwords of the 5-digit lock.
4. Pincodes use 6 digit slots, so at most 10 to the power 6 different pincodes are possible.

content.text:
Worked example: How many passwords does a lock with 6 slots of letters A to Z have? Compare it with a 5-digit lock, and say how many 6-digit pincodes are possible.
1. Each slot has 26 choices: 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26, which is 26 to the power 6.
2. 26 × 26 = 676, 676 × 676 = 456976, and 456976 × 676 = 308915776.
3. 308915776 ÷ 100000 is more than 3000, so the letter lock is much safer.
4. A pincode has 6 digit slots: 10 to the power 6, which is 1000000 possible codes.
Answer: 26 to the power 6, which is 308915776 passwords; up to 1000000 pincodes

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 11): A digital locker has an alphanumeric passcode of length 5. Some example codes are G89P0, 38098, BRJKW and 003AZ. How many such codes are possible?
1. Each slot can be one of 26 letters or 10 digits: 36 choices.
2. 5 slots: 36 × 36 × 36 × 36 × 36, which is 36 to the power 5.
3. 36 × 36 = 1296, 1296 × 36 = 46656, 46656 × 36 = 1679616, 1679616 × 36 = 60466176.
Answer: 36 to the power 5, which is 60466176 codes

concepts.concept_name: Power Play, Q9

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 9): A dairy plans to produce 8.5 billion packets of milk in a year. They want a unique ID code for each packet. If they choose to use the digits 0 to 9, how many digits should the code consist of?
1. n digit slots give 10 to the power n codes.
2. 8.5 billion is 8500000000, which is 8.5 × 10 to the power 9.
3. 10 to the power 9 is 1000000000, which is too few.
4. 10 to the power 10 is 10000000000, which is enough.
Answer: 10 digits

concepts.concept_name: Halving a line: 16, 8, 4, 2

content.text:
2.3 The Other Side of Powers
Imagine a line of length 16 units. Erasing half of it would result in 2⁴ ÷ 2 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 units.
Erasing half one more time would result in (2⁴ ÷ 2) ÷ 2 = 2⁴ ÷ 2² = 2 × 2 = 2² = 4 units.
Halving 16 cm three times may be written as 2⁴ ÷ 2³ = 2 units.

1. Predict first: after halving a 16-unit line three times, how long is it?

3. Halving twice divides by 2²: two factors cancel, leaving 2², which is 4.
4. Halving three times divides by 2³, leaving one factor of 2.

content.text:
Worked example: A line is 16 units long. Find its length after halving it once, twice and three times, as powers of 2.
1. 16 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which is 2⁴.
2. Once: 2⁴ ÷ 2 = 8, which is 2³.
3. Twice: 2⁴ ÷ 2² = 4, which is 2².
4. Three times: 2⁴ ÷ 2³ = 2, which is 2 to the power 1.
Answer: 8 units (2³), 4 units (2²) and 2 units (2 to the power 1)

media.title: Quotient Law Deriver
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Power Play, dividing powers of the same base. This is the mirror of the product law: joining two strips added the counts, so matching them across a bar takes the counts apart. It is read BEFORE zero and negative exponents, so the tool stops at the exact fraction and never writes 2 to the power minus 3, that notation belongs to the next two tools. NCERT derives this law by EXPANSION rather than stating it, which is why the numerator and denominator are drawn as separate factor blocks with a real × between them: the row of blocks IS the textbook figure. The word 'quotient' is never printed, because a Class 8 student has not met it; the tool says 'dividing powers with the same base'.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the cancelling that explains it.
whatYouLearned: a to the m over a to the n is a to the m minus n
A cancelled pair divides to 1, so cancelling never changes the value
Everything cancelling leaves 1, and a longer row below leaves an exact fraction

overview.goal: The student derives the quotient law by cancelling matched factors, and says that cancelling means dividing to one rather than deleting.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying one fraction bar, with a row of factor blocks above it and a row below it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says that when everything cancels nothing is left, and the bar holding one over one is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: In a quotient of powers of the same base, each factor above the bar can be matched with one below and each matched pair divides to 1. What is left is the difference in counts, so a to the m over a to the n equals a to the m minus n. When the denominator is longer the leftovers stay below the bar, which is a fraction and is where negative exponents begin.
overview.purpose: The student derives the quotient law by cancelling matched factors, and says that cancelling means dividing to one rather than deleting.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: The bar sits across the middle of the main panel with both rows centred on it and the value readout directly beneath. On a 390 px frame the rows wrap in pairs so a factor and its partner stay vertically aligned. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the result while a prediction is still open, and never draw a cancelled pair as an empty space. An empty space is the deletion misconception rendered.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A factor above the bar and a matching factor below make a to the 1 over a to the 1, which is 1, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing. Removing matched pairs therefore never changes the value, only the way it is written. What survives is however many factors could not find a partner, that is m minus n of them, and the sign of that difference says which side of the bar they are on. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): Cancelling divides a pair to one, so a fully cancelled fraction is 1. Breaks: Cancelling treated as deleting, so a fully cancelled fraction is read as nothing or as 0. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): When the denominator is longer the leftovers stay below the bar and the value is an exact fraction. Breaks: Believing the subtraction must be taken the larger way round so the answer comes out a whole number. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Cancelling removes pairs one at a time, which is subtraction and not division. Breaks: Quotient exponents divided rather than subtracted. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): An empty denominator cancels nothing, so dividing by a to the 0 leaves the power alone. Breaks: Believing a bar always removes something, so an empty denominator is read as an error. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Cancelling rewrites the fraction without moving its value, because each pair divides to one. Breaks: Cancelling treated as deleting, so the value is expected to shrink as pairs go.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each cancelled pair is a to the 1 over a to the 1, which is 1, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The value readout pulses but does not change as pair after pair cancels
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Cancelling is a rewriting, so the law reports what is left rather than what was removed

observationsAndConclusions.why: The pair divides to one, and one is a number that is still on the page
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A cancelled block is redrawn carrying a 1 and never as an empty space
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Everything cancelling leaves 1 over 1, which is why a to the 0 is going to be 1 and not nothing

observationsAndConclusions.why: Only m minus n factors can find a partner, and the sign of that difference says which side the leftovers are on
observationsAndConclusions.observe: When the row below is longer, blocks are left underneath the bar rather than above it
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A negative exponent is not a new rule; it is the same count coming out the other way

media.description: A fraction bar carries a row of factor blocks above it and a row below, both rows drawn from ONE unit and ONE left origin so factor i above sits exactly over factor i below. Tapping a factor above and then one below cancels them as a pair: both are struck through in grey, each is redrawn carrying a small orange 1, and one dashed link joins them across the bar so a pair reads as one cancellation and not as two. The value read-out is computed from the base and the two counts alone, never from how many pairs have gone, so it visibly refuses to move as pair after pair cancels, the invariant is a property of the compute rather than a claim in a caption. A cancel is refused with the reason printed when there is nothing below the bar to pair with, and refused again when the two bases differ, because only matching bases divide to 1. Setting the counts equal leaves the bar holding 1 over 1 and the strip reads 3³ ÷ 3³ = 27 ÷ 27 = 1; setting the lower count higher leaves the survivors below the bar and the result is written as an exact fraction and never as a decimal. Under the fraction a one-line working strip states the whole calculation in the textbook's own form, 3⁵ ÷ 3² = 243 ÷ 9 = 3³, with real × and ÷ characters and true superscripts, typeset by hand because the classroom renderer has no katex.

modes.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets m and n from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the cancelling, what is left and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
modes.normal: Free Play, student operated. The student sets m and n freely, cancels and uncancels any pair, and watches what is left above or below the bar. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.
modes.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own fraction. Simplify a quotient of powers, give the value when everything cancels, or give the exact fraction when the denominator is longer. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the cancelling that settles it.

concept.notation: Write a to the m over a to the n. A cancelled pair is written as 1, never crossed out and dropped, because it divides to one rather than disappearing.
concept.statement: In a quotient of powers of the same base, each factor above the bar can be matched with one below and each matched pair divides to 1. What is left is the difference in counts, so a to the m over a to the n equals a to the m minus n. When the denominator is longer the leftovers stay below the bar, which is a fraction and is where negative exponents begin.
prerequisites: a power as a count of factors
equivalent fractions and dividing a number by itself
misconceptions: Cancelling treated as deleting rather than as dividing to one, so a fully cancelled fraction is read as nothing rather than as 1.
Quotient exponents divided rather than subtracted, so a to the 6 over a to the 2 is taken as a cubed.
concept.why_it_is_true: A factor above the bar and a matching factor below make a to the 1 over a to the 1, which is 1, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing. Removing matched pairs therefore never changes the value, only the way it is written. What survives is however many factors could not find a partner, that is m minus n of them, and the sign of that difference says which side of the bar they are on.
worked_numbers: 5 threes over 2 threes cancels to 3 threes, so 3 to the 5 over 3 squared is 3 cubed, that is 27.
3 threes over 3 threes cancels completely and the value is 1, not 0 and not nothing.
2 threes over 5 threes leaves 3 threes below the bar, so the value is 1 over 27, written exactly and never as 0.037.

answer_key.worked: a to the m over a to the n is a to the m minus n. Every cancelled pair is a 1, so cancelling changes the writing and not the value.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn fraction: the result exponent from the surviving factors, the value 1 when everything cancels, or the exact fraction when the denominator is longer.
answer_key.precision: Results are kept as exact rationals when the exponent is negative. A value such as 1 over 8 is never shown as 0.125 and no graded value is held as a float.
answer_key.ground_truth: resultExponent(m, n) = m - n. sameBase required for any cancelling. valueAsRational(a, m, n) = {num: a to the max(m-n,0), den: a to the max(n-m,0)}, held as exact integers or BigInt. isNegativeForm(m, n) = n > m.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Everything cancels and the bar is left holding 1 over 1. The tool writes 1, not an empty space, and asks the student to say what it equals before showing it. This is the beat that produces the zero exponent by argument.
The leftovers stay below the bar and the result is an exact fraction. The tool never rewrites it as a decimal and never claims the exponent cannot be written.
The pair refuses to cancel and the refusal is surfaced with the reason. Only matching bases divide to one, and the refusal is where that is taught.
There is nothing below the bar, so nothing cancels and the value is unchanged. The tool draws the empty denominator rather than removing the bar.

edge_cases.case: A cancel that would change the value
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Impossible by construction. Cancelling only ever removes a matched pair, and the value readout is recomputed after every cancel to show it has not moved.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'simplify_quotient', base:number, m:number, n:number} | {kind:'full_cancel', base:number, m:number} | {kind:'exact_fraction', base:number, m:number, n:number} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

startingM.description: Factors above the bar, clamped 0 to 8.

startingN.description: Factors below the bar, clamped 0 to 8.

showValueReadout.description: Keep the value on screen through every cancel, so the student sees that cancelling does not move it.

constraints: Only matching bases can cancel. A tap pairing unlike bases is refused with the reason on screen rather than silently ignored.
Cancelling never changes the value shown. The value is recomputed after every cancel from the surviving factors, so the invariant is demonstrated and not merely asserted.
Results with a negative exponent are kept as exact rationals. 1 over 8 is never presented as 0.125, in any mode.
A cancelled pair is drawn as a 1, not removed from the scene, so cancelling reads as dividing to one rather than as deleting.
Values beyond 2 to the 53 use BigInt for both numerator and denominator so an exact fraction is always printable.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The fraction bar with both factor rows, the value readout, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: 5 threes sit above the bar and 2 below, nothing cancelled and the result HIDDEN. The class commits how many threes will be left out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Cancel: the matching pairs grey out one at a time, each becoming a visible 1, and three threes are left above the bar.
Everything cancels: m is set equal to n, the bar is left holding 1 over 1, and the class has to say what that equals before the tool writes it.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and the fully cancelled fraction has been named. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: 5 threes above the bar and 2 below, nothing cancelled, no result shown, the predict pad open on 'There are 5 threes on top and 2 threes below. How many threes will be left after cancelling?'.

normal.shows: The fraction, the value readout, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: 5 threes over 2 threes, nothing cancelled, with every control live.
play_modes: HOLD THE VALUE: cancel every pair in turn and watch the value readout, then say why it never moves.
EMPTY BAR: set the bottom count to 0 and say how many pairs cancel.
FLIP THE FRACTION: find three settings where the leftovers end up below the bar rather than above it.
ONE OVER ONE: cancel a fraction completely and say what the bar is left holding.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting m equal to n on the spot when a child asks what happens if everything goes.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the pairing visible before any arithmetic is done. Five 3s stand above the bar and two below, nothing cancelled, and the class is asked OUT LOUD how many threes will be left. The value 27 is already on screen, which is deliberate: it is the number the rest of the demonstration will show refusing to move.

Beat 2 is the argument in one motion. Two pairs cancel, each pair greying together and each block flipping to a 1, and the value read-out is recomputed from the base and the counts, so it cannot move, and the class watches it not move. Point at the read-out before you say anything about it.

Beat 3 carries the idea to its edge. The counts are set equal, every pair cancels, and the bar is left holding 1 over 1. Ask what that is worth before reading the strip: the answer 1 has to be produced by argument, because the whole misconception this tool exists to break is that a fully cancelled fraction is worth nothing.

media.instructions_for_student: Tap a factor above the bar, then a factor below it, and watch the pair cancel. Neither block disappears: each is struck through and drawn as a 1, because 3 over 3 is 1 and multiplying by 1 changes nothing. Keep an eye on the value while you cancel, it never moves. When every pair has gone the bar is left holding 1 over 1, which is 1, and when the row below is the longer one the leftovers stay below the bar and the answer is an exact fraction.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students use halving on a line of 16 units once, twice and three times, and write each length as a power of 2 as they cancel and divide out factors of 2.

Students generalise the halving pattern: to divide powers of the same base, subtract the exponents. They use it for 2 to the power 100 divided by 2 to the power 25 and explain why the base cannot be 0.
Students rewrite 4 to the power 32 as a power of 2, divide 2 to the power 224 by it by subtracting exponents, and find the units digit from the cycle of units digits of powers of 2.

concepts.concept_name: Why a power with exponent 0 is 1

content.text:
We have not covered the case when the exponent is 0; for example, what is 2 to the power 0?
Let us define 2 to the power 0 in a way that the generalised form above holds true.
2 to the power 0 is 2 to the power 4 − 4, which is 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴, and 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ = 1.
In general, x to the power a ÷ x to the power a = x to the power a − a = x to the power 0, and so 1 = x to the power 0, where x ≠ 0 and a is a counting number.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 2 to the power 0 equal to 0, to 1, or to 2?
2. Any number divided by itself is 1, so 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ is 1.
3. The rule says 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ is 2 to the power 4 − 4, which is 2 to the power 0.
4. For the rule to stay true, 2 to the power 0 must be 1, and the same holds for any nonzero base.

content.text:
Worked example: Use 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ to decide the value of 2 to the power 0, and then find 5 to the power 0 and 10 to the power 0.
1. 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ is 16 ÷ 16, which is 1, since every factor cancels.
2. By the division rule, 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ is 2 to the power 4 − 4, which is 2 to the power 0.
3. So 2 to the power 0 must be 1, not 0.
4. In the same way 5³ ÷ 5³ is 1, so 5 to the power 0 is 1, and 10 to the power 0 is 1.
Answer: 2 to the power 0, 5 to the power 0 and 10 to the power 0 are all 1

concepts.concept_name: Halving past 1: negative exponents

content.text:
When Zero is in Power!
When a line of length 2⁴ units is halved 5 times, 2⁴ ÷ 2 to the power 5 gives 1/2 units.
Using the generalised form, we get 2⁴ ÷ 2 to the power 5 as 2 to the power (4 − 5), which is 2 to the power −1. So, 2 to the power −1 is 1/2.
When a line of length 2⁴ units is halved 10 times, we get 2⁴ ÷ 2 to the power 10 as 2 to the power (4 − 10), which is 2 to the power −6 units.
When expanded, the 4 factors above cancel 4 of the 10 below, leaving 1 over 2 to the power 6, which is 1/64, also written as 2 to the power −6.

content.text:
Worked example: A line is 16 units long. Find its length after halving it 5 times and 10 times, as a fraction and as a power of 2.
1. Halving 5 times: 16 ÷ 32 = 1/2.
2. By the rule, 2⁴ ÷ 2 to the power 5 is 2 to the power −1, so 2 to the power −1 is 1/2.
3. Halving 10 times: 16 ÷ 1024 = 1/64.
4. By the rule, 2⁴ ÷ 2 to the power 10 is 2 to the power −6, so 2 to the power −6 is 1/64.
Answer: 1/2 unit, which is 2 to the power −1, and 1/64 unit, which is 2 to the power −6

concepts.concept_name: Negative powers are reciprocals

content.text:
Similarly, 10 to the power −3 is 1/10³, 7 to the power −2 is 1/7², etc.
Can we write 10³ as 1 over 10 to the power −3? We can write 1 over 10 to the power −3 as 1 ÷ (1/10³), and 1 ÷ (1/10³) = 1 × 10³ = 10³.
In a generalised form, n to the power −a = 1 over n to the power a, and n to the power a = 1 over n to the power −a, where n ≠ 0.

Worked example: Simplify: 2 to the power −4 × 2 to the power 7; 3² × 3 to the power −5 × 3 to the power 6; p³ × p to the power −10; 2⁴ × (−4) to the power −2; 8 to the power p × 8 to the power q.
1. Add exponents: −4 + 7 = 3, so 2³.
2. 2 + (−5) + 6 = 3, so 3³.
3. 3 + (−10) = −7, so p to the power −7.
4. (−4) to the power −2 is 1/16, so 2⁴ × 1/16 = 16/16 = 1, which is 2 to the power 0.
5. Add the exponents: 8 to the power p + q.
Answer: 2³, 3³, p to the power −7, 1, and 8 to the power p + q

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 5): Simplify and write these in the exponential form. (i) 10 to the power −2 × 10 to the power −5 (ii) 5 to the power 7 ÷ 5⁴ (iii) 9 to the power −7 ÷ 9⁴ (iv) (13 to the power −2) to the power −3 (v) m to the power 5 n to the power 12 (mn) to the power 9
1. (i) Add the exponents: −2 + (−5) = −7, so 10 to the power −7.
2. (ii) Subtract: 7 − 4 = 3, so 5³.
3. (iii) Subtract: −7 − 4 = −11, so 9 to the power −11.
4. (iv) Multiply: −2 × −3 = 6, so 13 to the power 6.
5. (v) (mn) to the power 9 is m to the power 9 n to the power 9; add: m to the power 14 n to the power 21.
Answer: (i) 10 to the power −7 (ii) 5³ (iii) 9 to the power −11 (iv) 13 to the power 6 (v) m to the power 14 n to the power 21

media.title: Zero Exponent Staircase
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash 'Power Play', the zero exponent, met immediately after the quotient law and the fully cancelled fraction. The class has already seen a power as a count of factors and aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = 1; what it has not seen is the descending table carried one row further. This tool sits on the Justify beat: the pattern is watched arriving at the same place from above, so a⁰ = 1 is FORCED rather than announced. Negative exponents are the next tool and the staircase deliberately hands over to it rather than stopping at 1.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the staircase that explains it.
whatYouLearned: Each step down the staircase divides by the base, because it removes one factor
a to the 0 is 1 for every base other than zero
The reason never mentions the base, which is why one argument settles them all

overview.goal: The student continues a descending pattern to justify the value of a power with exponent zero, and says why the answer is one for any non zero base.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a staircase of value cards descending to the right, each pair of steps joined by a labelled dividing arrow. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is split between a power with exponent zero being zero and being the base itself, and the dividing staircase is asked where the next step lands.
overview.concept: Each step down the staircase divides by the base, because dropping the exponent by one removes one factor. Continuing that from a to the 1, which is a, gives a divided by a, which is 1. So a to the 0 is 1 for every non zero base. Nothing about the base enters the argument, which is why the answer does not depend on it.
overview.purpose: The student continues a descending pattern to justify the value of a power with exponent zero, and says why the answer is one for any non zero base.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Staircase fills the main panel with the exponent printed beside each step and the base selector beneath. On a 390 px frame the top steps scroll out of view while the last three and the empty slot stay pinned, because the bottom is where the argument is. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not write the value of the zero exponent step while a prediction is still open, and never present it as a stated rule. The dividing arrow IS the justification.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The staircase is built by one rule: each step is the previous divided by the base. That rule is not a convention, it is what removing a factor does. Applying it to the step a to the 1, whose value is a, gives a over a, and any non zero number divided by itself is 1. Because the argument never mentions which number a is, it settles every base at once. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The landing at 1 does not depend on the values shrinking, so a flat staircase is not a broken one. Breaks: Believing the landing on 1 comes from the values getting smaller, so a staircase that never shrinks is read as failing. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): The rule a to the 0 is 1 holds for every base except 0, and the staircase shows exactly why. Breaks: Believing a to the 0 is 1 for absolutely every base, base 0 included. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): The landing is forced by the dividing rule, not by the size of the base. Breaks: Believing a to the 0 is a separate fact that has to be memorised for each base. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The exponent 0 is a step on the way down, not the bottom of the staircase. Breaks: Believing the pattern ends at the exponent 0 because the whole numbers have run out. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A zero exponent means no factors are multiplied, and the product of no factors is 1, never 0. Breaks: 2 to the power 0 taken as 0, on the reading that a zero exponent removes the number.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the base 2 staircase reading 16, 8, 4, 2 with the next slot empty, and ask the class to say out loud what comes next and what the zero exponent step will be. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets base 2 with four steps shown. Never drop the next step before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Drop the next step so its dividing arrow draws itself first and the value it forces lands beside the committed guess. Point at the arrow label and then at the bottom step. Targets base 2 at the exponent zero. Read the landed value from getState().truth. Call 3. Rebuild the staircase at base 5 and then at base 10, and before base 7 is drawn ask the class whether the landing will be the same. Targets base 5, base 10 and then base 7. Read each landing from the tool's own readout, never from this plan.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Removing one factor from a power is exactly dividing by the base once
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Every arrow on the staircase carries the same instruction, divide by the base
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The staircase is built by one rule, so the last step is not a special case that needs its own rule

observationsAndConclusions.why: The final step is the base divided by itself, and any number other than zero divided by itself is 1
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Changing the base rewrites every card but the bottom card still reads 1
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The argument settles every base at once, which is why the answer does not depend on the base

observationsAndConclusions.why: The dividing step would be a division by zero, so the staircase cannot be built at all
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Base zero is refused rather than drawn
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The one base excluded is excluded for a reason that is on the arrow, not by decree

media.description: A staircase of value cards descends to the right, one card per exponent, each card carrying NCERT's two columns, the index form beside its value, so the card reads 2³ = 8 rather than a bare 8, and each pair of cards joined by an arrow whose pill states the rule as ÷ the base. Every column of the scene shares ONE exponent axis, so two staircases of different heights land on the SAME row and the claim that the base does not move the landing is true in the drawing rather than asserted beside it. The base can be rebuilt from 0 to 10: at base 1 the staircase is flat and still lands on 1, and at base 0 the machinery visibly jams at the arrow, a ÷ 0 pill drawn above a dashed slot that reads no value, instead of the base being greyed out on a selector. Free Play docks an empty step under the last one and checks a typed value against the previous value divided by the base rather than against a stored fact, refusing a wrong entry by highlighting the arrow and never by stating the answer, and the descent carries on past the exponent 0 into 1/3 and 1/9 drawn as real stacked fractions. Practice renders the scene each bank question describes, the stated staircase, the product's other factor, the four powers to be ordered, masks only the quantity the item asks for until the check, and grades every answer against the value the drawn scene itself computes.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the base from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the staircase, the dividing arrow and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the staircase 16, 8, 4, 2 and the next step EMPTY, and asks what comes next and what 2 to the 0 will be. Beat 3 changes the base to 5 and then to 10, and the class is asked whether the answer would still be one for base 7 before base 7 is shown. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setBase, dropStep and say.

concept.notation: Write a to the 0. The exponent 0 means no factors are multiplied, and the product of no factors is 1.
concept.statement: Each step down the staircase divides by the base, because dropping the exponent by one removes one factor. Continuing that from a to the 1, which is a, gives a divided by a, which is 1. So a to the 0 is 1 for every non zero base. Nothing about the base enters the argument, which is why the answer does not depend on it.
prerequisites: a power as a count of factors
the quotient law and a fully cancelled fraction
misconceptions: 2 to the 0 taken as 0, on the reading that a zero exponent removes the number.
2 to the 0 taken as 2, on the reading that a zero exponent does nothing at all.
concept.why_it_is_true: The staircase is built by one rule: each step is the previous divided by the base. That rule is not a convention, it is what removing a factor does. Applying it to the step a to the 1, whose value is a, gives a over a, and any non zero number divided by itself is 1. Because the argument never mentions which number a is, it settles every base at once.
worked_numbers: Base 2: 16, 8, 4, 2, then 1, so 2 to the 0 is 1.
Base 5: 625, 125, 25, 5, then 1, so the same landing from a different height.
Base 10: 1000, 100, 10, then 1, which is the step that makes the place value columns line up.

extra: A length halved again and again until the halvings run out
A price cut by the same fraction each week, read back to the week nothing had happened
A tank drained to a tenth each hour, traced back to the hour it was full
A folded sheet unfolded once for every fold, back to the flat sheet
A photocopy of a photocopy traced back to the original page
A savings amount stepped back year by year to the day it was deposited
textbook: The descending list of powers of 2 continued down to the exponent zero
A quotient of two equal powers, which is 1 and is also a power with exponent zero
The place value columns written as powers of ten, ending at the units column

answer_key.worked: a to the 0 is 1 for every non zero base, because each step down divides by the base and a divided by a is 1.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn staircase: the value of the zero exponent step, the value of a product containing one, or whether a stated reason appeals to the pattern rather than to a rule.
answer_key.precision: Exact integer arithmetic throughout, with BigInt above 2 to the 53. Each step is computed as the previous divided exactly by the base, never as a rounded quotient.
answer_key.ground_truth: step(a, k) = a to the k, computed exactly. nextStep(v, a) = v / a as an exact division, defined only when a is non zero. value(a, 0) = 1 for every a not equal to 0. 0 to the 0 is refused as undefined here.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

a predict verb in windowMethods

visual_behaviour.never: Do not write the value of the zero exponent step while a prediction is still open, and never present it as a stated rule. The dividing arrow IS the justification.
visual_behaviour.scene: A vertical staircase of value cards descending to the right, each pair joined by a labelled arrow reading divide by the base. Filled steps take the primary accent, the step being set takes the second, and the empty next step is an outlined slot.
visual_behaviour.layout: Staircase fills the main panel with the exponent printed beside each step and the base selector beneath. On a 390 px frame the top steps scroll out of view while the last three and the empty slot stay pinned, because the bottom is where the argument is.
readouts: The base and the current bottom exponent, always on screen
The dividing rule as words on every arrow
Which bases have been tried and where each landed, once more than one has been used
animations: Step drop: the new step falls into its slot over 200 ms and its arrow draws itself, so the rule arrives before the number.
Base rebuild: the values transform in place over 320 ms while the staircase shape and the landing point stay fixed, which is what makes the independence from the base visible.
Landing: when the step reaches the exponent zero the card pulses once and holds, marking the end of the descent rather than announcing a rule.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Step card width is derived from the panel width and the longest value string so no value is ever truncated; when a value grows past the card the staircase scrolls its top out of view rather than shrinking the type.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The dividing arrow has to be watched forcing the next value before the zero exponent is named, or the answer arrives as a convention to be accepted rather than as the only value the pattern allows

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the rule arrives before the number. Every arrow on the staircase carries the same instruction, ÷ the base, and the bottom card is simply what that instruction produces at the exponent 0. Ask the class out loud what comes after 16, 8, 4, 2 before you read the bottom card, then point at the arrow rather than at the value: the arrow is the justification, and naming a⁰ = 1 as a rule at this beat throws the argument away.

Beat 2 is the whole proof in one row of the picture. The value at the exponent 1 is the base itself, so the last step is the base divided by itself, and the second strip line shows the same thing arriving from the quotient law, 2³ ÷ 2³ = 2⁰, which the class met last lesson. Two routes, one landing.

Beat 3 is where the generalisation is earned rather than stated. Every value on the screen changes as the base moves and the bottom row does not, because the argument never named which number the base was. Ask whether base 7 would land anywhere else BEFORE calling setBase(7), so the class commits and the tool settles it.

media.title: What should two to the power zero be?

media.title: What does a negative exponent do to a power?

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students define 2 to the power 0 so that the division rule still works, showing that 2⁴ divided by 2⁴ is 1, and generalise that x to the power 0 is 1 for any nonzero x.
Students continue halving a 16-unit line 5 times and 10 times, get half a unit and one sixty-fourth of a unit, and write these lengths with negative exponents as powers of 2.
Students write 10 to the power −3 and 7 to the power −2 as fractions, show that 10 cubed is 1 over 10 to the power −3, and check that the exponent rules also hold for integer exponents.
Students write 2 to the power −4, 10 to the power −5, (−7) to the power −2, (−5) to the power −3 and 10 to the power −100 as one over a positive power.
Students simplify products of powers that have negative exponents by adding the exponents, including 2⁴ × (−4) to the power −2 and 8 to the power p times 8 to the power q.
Students simplify products, quotients and powers of powers with negative exponents into exponential form, and write one number as a product of powers in three different ways.

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 3): Write the given number as the product of two or more powers in three different ways. The powers can be any integers. (i) 64³ (ii) 192 to the power 8 (iii) 32 to the power −5
1. (i) 64³ is 2 to the power 18: 2 to the power 10 × 2 to the power 8, 4 to the power 5 × 4⁴, and 8³ × 8³.
2. (ii) 192 is 2 to the power 6 × 3, so 192 to the power 8 is 2 to the power 48 × 3 to the power 8; also 64 to the power 8 × 3 to the power 8, and 12 to the power 8 × 16 to the power 8.
3. (iii) 32 to the power −5 is 2 to the power −25: 2 to the power −10 × 2 to the power −15, 4 to the power −5 × 8 to the power −5, and 2 to the power 5 × 2 to the power −30.
Answer: For example (i) 2 to the power 10 × 2 to the power 8, 4 to the power 5 × 4⁴, 8³ × 8³ (ii) 2 to the power 48 × 3 to the power 8, 64 to the power 8 × 3 to the power 8, 12 to the power 8 × 16 to the power 8 (iii) 2 to the power −10 × 2 to the power −15, 4 to the power −5 × 8 to the power −5, 2 to the power 5 × 2 to the power −30

<bookmark mark='base'/>Step one, make the base two. Sixty four is two to the power six.
<bookmark mark='exp'/>Six times three is eighteen, so the number is two to the power eighteen.
<bookmark mark='w1'/>Break eighteen into ten plus eight.
<bookmark mark='w2'/>Four to the power nine works too, with nine as five plus four.
<bookmark mark='w3'/>Eight to the power six works too, with six as three plus three.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Step two, one hundred and ninety two is sixty four times three. That is two to the power six times three.
<bookmark mark='eight'/>Each factor gets the power eight. That gives two to the power forty eight times three to the power eight.
<bookmark mark='w2'/>Two to the power six is sixty four. Keeping it gives sixty four to the power eight times three to the power eight.
<bookmark mark='w3'/>Also, one hundred and ninety two is twelve times sixteen. That gives twelve to the power eight times sixteen to the power eight.
<bookmark mark='base'/>Step three, thirty two is two to the power five.
<bookmark mark='exp'/>Five times negative five is negative twenty five.
<bookmark mark='w1'/>Break negative twenty five into negative ten plus negative fifteen.
<bookmark mark='w2'/>Four times eight is thirty two. That gives four to the power negative five times eight to the power negative five.
<bookmark mark='w3'/>Or break negative twenty five into five plus negative thirty.

concepts.concept_name: The power line of 4

content.text:
Power Lines
Let us arrange the powers of 4 along a line.
4 to the power 8 is 65536, 4 to the power 7 is 16384, 4 to the power 6 is 4096, 4 to the power 5 is 1024, 4⁴ is 256, 4³ is 64, 4² is 16, 4 to the power 1 is 4, 4 to the power 0 is 1, 4 to the power −1 is 1/4 and 4 to the power −2 is 1/16.
4 to the power 8 ÷ 4³, 4³ × 4², 4 to the power 7 × 4 to the power −2; 65536 ÷ 64, 64 × 16, 16384 ÷ 16.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 65536 ÷ 64 a power of 4?
2. Each step up the line multiplies by 4; each step down divides by 4.
3. 65536 is 4 to the power 8 and 64 is 4³: dividing moves 3 steps down to 4 to the power 5, 1024.
4. 64 × 16 moves 2 steps up from 4³, landing on 4 to the power 5 again.

content.text:
Worked example: Use the power line of 4 to find 65536 ÷ 64, 64 × 16 and 16384 ÷ 16 as powers of 4.
1. 65536 is 4 to the power 8 and 64 is 4³: 8 − 3 = 5, so 4 to the power 5. Check: 65536 ÷ 64 = 1024.
2. 64 is 4³ and 16 is 4²: 3 + 2 = 5, so 4 to the power 5. Check: 64 × 16 = 1024.
3. 16384 is 4 to the power 7 and 16 is 4²: 7 − 2 = 5. Check: 16384 ÷ 16 = 1024.
4. 4 to the power 7 × 4 to the power −2 also lands on 4 to the power 5.
Answer: All three are 4 to the power 5, which is 1024

concepts.concept_name: How many times larger?

content.text:
Can we say that 16384 (4 to the power 7) is 16 (4²) times larger than 1024 (4 to the power 5)?
Yes, since 4 to the power 7 ÷ 4 to the power 5 is 4².
How many times larger than 4 to the power −2 is 4²?

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 4² four times larger than 4 to the power −2, or many more times?
2. How many times larger is a quotient: divide the larger power by the smaller one.
3. 4 to the power 7 ÷ 4 to the power 5 is 4², so 16384 is 16 times 1024.
4. 4² ÷ 4 to the power −2 is 4 to the power 2 − (−2), which is 4⁴, which is 256 times.

content.text:
Worked example: Show that 16384 is 16 times 1024, and find how many times larger 4² is than 4 to the power −2.
1. 16384 is 4 to the power 7 and 1024 is 4 to the power 5.
2. 4 to the power 7 ÷ 4 to the power 5 is 4², which is 16. Check: 16384 ÷ 1024 = 16.
3. 4² ÷ 4 to the power −2 is 4 to the power 2 − (−2), which is 4⁴.
4. Check: 16 ÷ (1/16) = 16 × 16 = 256, and 4⁴ = 256.
Answer: 16384 is 16 times 1024; 4² is 4⁴, which is 256, times 4 to the power −2

tool_config.title: Power Line Walker
tool_config.idea: On a power line each step up multiplies by the base and each step down divides by it, so multiplying powers moves along the line by adding exponents, and dividing moves back by subtracting them.
tool_config.screen: A power line for a chosen base, with the powers from the base to the power −4 up to the base to the power 7 as labelled stops and a token on one stop. Move cards show multiply by or divide by a power of the base, and the token jumps the matching number of steps.
student_does: Read the stop the token stands on and the move card.
Predict the stop the token will land on.
Play the move card and watch the token jump.
Read the landing stop as a power and as a number.
challenges: Start at 4 to the power 3 and multiply by 4 squared: where does the token land?
Start at 4 to the power 6 and divide by 4 to the power 4: where does it land?
Start at 4 squared and divide by 4 to the power 5: where does it land?
On the power line of 3, start at 3 to the power 5 and divide by 3 to the power 7: where does it land?
How many times larger is 4 to the power 7 than 4 cubed?
How many times larger is 4 than 4 to the power −2?
feedback: A landing found by multiplying the exponents is tested and shown to miss the right stop.
A move down past 1 lands on a fraction stop and shows it as 1 over a power.
Each landing is checked by working out both numbers and dividing.
tool_config.done_when: All six cards are done with each landing predicted before the token moves.

The token is moved to the right stop and the power is read, then a new card follows.

concepts.concept_name: Expanded form with powers of 10

content.text:
2.4 Powers of 10
We have used numbers like 10, 100, 1000, and so on when writing Indian numerals in an expanded form. For example, 47561 = (4 × 10000) + (7 × 1000) + (5 × 100) + (6 × 10) + 1.
This can be written using powers of 10 as (4 × 10⁴) + (7 × 10³) + (5 × 10²) + (6 × 10 to the power 1) + (1 × 10 to the power 0).
Write these numbers in the same way: (i) 172, (ii) 5642, (iii) 6374.
How can we write 561.903? Writing it using powers of 10, we have 561.903 as (5 × 10²) + (6 × 10 to the power 1) + (1 × 10 to the power 0) + (9 × 10 to the power −1) + (0 × 10 to the power −2) + (3 × 10 to the power −3).

concepts.concept_name: Scientific notation for very large numbers

content.text:
Scientific Notation
Let's look at some facts involving large numbers: (i) The Sun is located 300000000000000000000 m from the centre of our Milky Way galaxy. (ii) The number of stars in our galaxy is 100000000000. (iii) The mass of the Earth is 5976000000000000000000000 kg.
As the number of digits increases, it becomes difficult to read the numbers correctly. We may miscount the number of zeroes.
For example, the number 5900 can be expressed as 590 × 10, 59 × 10², 5.9 × 10³ or 0.59 × 10⁴.
Any number can be written as the product of a number between 1 and 10 and a power of 10.
In scientific notation or scientific form (also called standard form), we write numbers as x × 10 to the power y, where x ≥ 1 and x < 10 is the coefficient and y, the exponent, is any integer.

Worked example: Write 5900 in four ways using powers of 10, and write the three large-number facts in scientific notation.
1. 5900 is 590 × 10, 59 × 10², 5.9 × 10³ and 0.59 × 10⁴. Only 5.9 × 10³ has a coefficient from 1 up to 10.
2. The Sun's distance is 3 followed by 20 zeroes, so 3 × 10 to the power 20 m.

concepts.concept_name: The exponent matters more than the coefficient

content.text:
Often, the exponent y is more important than the coefficient x. When we write the 2 crore population of Mumbai as 2 × 10 to the power 7, the 7 is more important than the 2.
If the 2 is changed to 3, the population increases by one-half, i.e., 2 crore to 3 crore, whereas if the 7 is changed to 8, the change in population is 10 times, i.e., 2 crores to 20 crores.
If we say that the population of Kohima is 142395, then it gives the impression that we are quite sure about this number up to the units place. If we are only sure that the population is around 1 lakh 42 thousand, we can write it as 1.42 × 10 to the power 5.
The number of digits in the coefficient reflects how well we know the number.
How old is this dinosaur's skeleton? It is 70 million and 15 years old... when I started working here, it was 70 million years old.

3. So the Sun to Earth distance, with exponent 11, is the smallest even though 1.496 looks largest.

media.title: Power Comparison Duel
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Exponents and Powers, the Powers of Ten segment - place value, standard form and comparison. This closes the chapter: the product law, the power of a power law, a to the power 0 and negative exponents have all been met, so the duel is where the student chooses which law applies rather than being told. It rehearses the 1 mark 'which is larger' board reading and the 2 mark rewrite item directly, and it is the mount that breaks the two comparison misconceptions the chapter names.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's pick, the student's reason, the valid reasons, and both values.
whatYouLearned: With a shared base the larger exponent wins, and with a shared exponent the larger base wins
Rewriting a card onto a common footing turns a comparison into ordinary size
A bigger base on its own is not evidence about which value is larger

overview.goal: The student decides which of two powers is larger and justifies the choice by rewriting to a common base or exponent rather than by guessing.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with two power cards dealt side by side, their value panels blank, and a list of reasons beneath them. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class backs the card with the bigger base without computing either value, and both cards stay face down until a reason is given.
overview.concept: Two powers can be compared without full evaluation by putting them on a common footing. With the same base, the larger exponent wins. With the same exponent, the larger base wins. Otherwise one card must be rewritten so that a base or an exponent is shared, and only then does a comparison follow. A bigger base alone and a bigger exponent alone decide nothing.
overview.purpose: The student decides which of two powers is larger and justifies the choice by rewriting to a common base or exponent rather than by guessing.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Cards fill the upper main panel side by side, reason list directly beneath, scoreboard to the right on a wide frame and collapsed to a strip under the reasons on a 390 px frame. Every reason row keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal either value before the reason is submitted, and never display or reward elapsed time. A revealed value turns the duel into arithmetic and a timer turns it into a race.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Powers grow by multiplication, so the two numbers in a card interact rather than competing separately. Rewriting to a common base or a common exponent makes one of them cancel out of the decision, and what is left is a comparison of single numbers, which can be settled by ordinary size. Without such a rewrite, neither number in the card is by itself evidence about the value. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A bigger base is not by itself evidence about the value of a card. Breaks: Comparing by the bigger base alone, so 5 to the power 3 is taken as the larger card. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Equal is a legitimate outcome, because two different writings can name one value. Breaks: Believing a duel must always have a winner, so two powers are never allowed to coincide. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Each shortcut needs a shared field, and without one neither number in a card is evidence. Breaks: Comparing by the bigger exponent alone, without checking whether the bases are comparable. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): Some pairs have no common footing, and saying so is the method rather than a failure. Breaks: Believing every pair can be rewritten onto a common base, so a rewrite is invented. conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with two cards dealt, both value panels blank and no reason chosen, and ask the class to say out loud which is larger and how they know. Commit the class pick and reason on the prediction pad. Targets the pair 2 to the power 10 against 10 cubed. Never reveal either value at this call. Call 2. Apply the committed reason so one card rewrites and the shared base or exponent lights up. Point at the rewritten card and then at the shared field. Targets the rewrite onto a common base. Say what the comparison has been reduced to, and read the rewritten form from the tool's own readout. Call 3. Reveal both values at once and set them beside the reason that was given. Targets both value panels. Read both values from getState().truth, never from this plan, and say whether the reason had settled the duel before the arithmetic was done.

observationsAndConclusions.why: If one landed first it would be read first, and the duel would be decided by arithmetic rather than by the reason
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Both value panels fill at exactly the same instant
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A comparison is a piece of reasoning, and the values are only its confirmation

observationsAndConclusions.why: Once a base is common, the two values differ only in their exponents, and single numbers can be ordered by size
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Rewriting one card so a base is shared makes the other number drop out of the decision
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The point of a rewrite is to remove one of the two numbers from the argument

observationsAndConclusions.why: The base and the exponent interact by multiplication, so neither one alone is evidence about the value
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A card with the bigger base can hold the smaller value
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Comparing on one number of a power is a habit that has to be given up, not adjusted

media.description: Two power cards are dealt side by side on a plain working ground, each showing a base with a raised exponent in large type and a value panel beneath it. Under the pair run two magnitude bars that start from ONE origin and use ONE unit, so their lengths are exactly proportional to the two values - which is why 2 to the power 10 and 10 to the power 3 draw as two bars a hair apart rather than as a rout. Concept walks three teaching beats: the pair whose bigger base loses by 24, the pair that rewrites onto one base until both cards read the same glyphs, and the pair that no rewrite reaches. Learn stages the five reviewed checkpoints, each opening with its answer and both values already on screen and taking no input at all. Practice serves six questions drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, masking both value panels until the attempt is in, then naming the reasons that genuinely settle that pair. Free Play is the duel itself: tap the card you believe is larger, choose a reason from the five, watch a valid rewrite transform a card with the shared field lighting up, and only then reveal both values - which fill at the same instant so neither is read first. A scoreboard records which reasons have been used. No elapsed time is displayed anywhere and none is scored.

scenes.onScreen: Both cards, the reason list, the scoreboard, every control, no score and no question. 2 to the 10 against 10 to the 3 with values hidden and every control live.

The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A card reads a to the n. Comparing cards means deciding which value is larger without necessarily computing either one.
concept.statement: Two powers can be compared without full evaluation by putting them on a common footing. With the same base, the larger exponent wins. With the same exponent, the larger base wins. Otherwise one card must be rewritten so that a base or an exponent is shared, and only then does a comparison follow. A bigger base alone and a bigger exponent alone decide nothing.
prerequisites: the product law and the power of a power law
powers of ten and orders of magnitude
misconceptions: Comparing by the bigger base alone, so 10 to the 3 is taken as larger than 2 to the 10.
Comparing by the bigger exponent alone, without checking whether the bases are comparable.
concept.why_it_is_true: Powers grow by multiplication, so the two numbers in a card interact rather than competing separately. Rewriting to a common base or a common exponent makes one of them cancel out of the decision, and what is left is a comparison of single numbers, which can be settled by ordinary size. Without such a rewrite, neither number in the card is by itself evidence about the value.
worked_numbers: 2 to the 10 is 1024 and 10 to the 3 is 1000, so the smaller base wins, which the bigger base reading gets exactly backwards.
2 to the 8 against 4 to the 4: rewriting 4 as 2 squared gives 2 to the 8 on both sides, so they are equal.
3 times 10 to the 8 against 9 times 10 to the 7: a whole decade separates them, so the exponent settles it before the coefficient is looked at.

extra: Two savings plans, one doubling for ten years and one growing tenfold for three
Two rumours, one told to two people a day and one told to ten people every third day
Two stacks of folded paper, folded different numbers of times from different starting thicknesses
Two colonies, one splitting in two every hour and one tripling every two hours
Two prize schemes, one paying a power of 3 and one a power of 9
Two file sizes written as powers of 2 and compared without expanding them
textbook: Two powers of ten compared by their exponents alone
A power of 2 compared with a power of ten of similar size
Two quantities in standard form compared exponent first
A power rewritten on a common base so two expressions can be set against each other

answer_key.worked: Compare the exponent first when the bases match and the base first when the exponents match; otherwise rewrite one card until something is shared, and only then decide.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the dealt pair: which card is larger by exact BigInt comparison, and whether the chosen reason is in the item's set of valid reason tags.
answer_key.precision: Both values are held as BigInt strings so a card such as 2 to the 40 compares exactly. No comparison is ever made on a float and no point is ever awarded for response time.
answer_key.ground_truth: value(a, n) = BigInt exponentiation. larger(cardA, cardB) = BigInt comparison of the two values, or 'equal'. validReasons(pair) = the tags that genuinely settle this pair, computed from whether the bases match, the exponents match, or a rewrite exists.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Equal is an allowed pick and the tool says so. Forcing a larger card would teach that two powers can never coincide, which 2 to the 8 against 4 to the 4 immediately disproves.

edge_cases.case: A correct pick with an invalid reason
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Scored as partially correct and a hint is triggered. The reason is the graded object, so a lucky pick cannot score full.

edge_cases.case: A pair where no rewrite exists
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Estimation is the only route and the tool says so, offering the bounding decade as the valid reason rather than pretending a rewrite is available.
Comparison is BigInt so 2 to the 40 style cards do not overflow, and the revealed values are printed in full rather than in exponential notation.

edge_cases.case: A student trying to reveal before reasoning
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked. Values are never revealed before the reason is submitted, because the whole design is to make the reason precede the arithmetic.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'duel', a:[number,number], b:[number,number], validReasons:string[]} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

startingPair.description: The pair the duel opens on, each card a base and an exponent.

showScoreboard.description: Show the running record of which reasons have been used. The scoreboard records reasons, never time taken.

constraints: Values are never revealed before the reason is submitted. This is the invariant the whole tool rests on.
Comparison uses BigInt so cards such as 2 to the 40 compare exactly and never overflow.
Points come from the reason and never from speed. No timer contributes to the score and none is displayed as a target.
A correct pick with an invalid reason scores as partially correct and triggers a hint rather than being marked simply wrong.
The scoreboard records which reasons have been used, so the student's record is a picture of their methods rather than of their pace.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The two cards, the reason list, the scoreboard, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: 2 to the 10 and 10 to the 3 are dealt with both values HIDDEN. The class commits which is larger and how they know, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Apply the reason: the committed reason is used, rewriting both cards onto a common base or exponent so the comparison becomes one of single numbers.
Reveal: both values appear, 1024 against 1000, and the reason is seen to have settled the duel before the arithmetic was done.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and both values are on screen beside the reason that predicted them. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: Two cards reading 2 to the 10 and 10 to the 3 with both values hidden and no reason chosen, the predict pad open on 'Which is larger, 2 to the 10 or 10 to the 3? Choose and say how you know before revealing.'.

play_modes: BASE TRAP: find three pairs where the card with the smaller base wins.
DEAD HEAT: deal pairs until you find two cards of exactly equal value, and say how you knew.
ONE REASON ONLY: settle four duels without ever using the same reason twice.
NO REWRITE: find a pair that no rewrite settles, and say what you used instead.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example dealing a pair a child proposes and applying the reason they offer to see whether it settles anything.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

practice.selection: Six served per load, one drawn at random from each slot's five item type. Composition is fixed and the specific question inside a slot is random, so repeat visits to the same tool show different questions.
practice.exclusions: Nothing shown solved in Learn is ever served here, checkpoints included. No question text repeats inside this mount. Practice values differ from the textbook's own printed problem values.
practice.source_prop: props.questions, drawn at random inside each slot's difficulty and subtype
practice.interaction_rules: At least 4 distinct interactions, none above 40 per cent, at least 2 per difficulty band, at most 4 the same inside one type of five.
practice.fallback_precedence: DIFFICULTY is fixed and never traded: a Hard slot serves a Hard question or nothing. SUBTYPE gives way second, because it decides what thinking the slot does. SOURCE gives way first, because provenance matters less than the kind of thinking.
