visual_behaviour.never: Do not reveal either value before the reason is submitted, and never display or reward elapsed time. A revealed value turns the duel into arithmetic and a timer turns it into a race.
visual_behaviour.scene: Two power cards dealt side by side, each showing a base and a raised exponent in large type with a blank value panel beneath. The picked card lifts and takes the primary accent. A reason list sits below, and a scoreboard of reasons used runs along the side.
visual_behaviour.layout: Cards fill the upper main panel side by side, reason list directly beneath, scoreboard to the right on a wide frame and collapsed to a strip under the reasons on a 390 px frame. Every reason row keeps a 44 px hit target.
readouts: Both cards in power form, always on screen
The committed pick and the chosen reason, once each is made
The reasons used so far, as a record of method rather than of pace
animations: Card lift: the picked card rises 8 px over 140 ms and holds, so a pick is felt as a commitment while the values are still hidden.
Rewrite: when a reason applies, one card transforms into its rewritten form over 320 ms with the shared base or exponent lighting up, which is the reason made visible.
Reveal: both value panels fill at the same instant so neither is read first, and the deciding field stays highlighted behind them.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Card size is derived from the panel width so both cards fit side by side with the exponent legible at half size on a 390 px frame; revealed values wrap within the panel rather than shrinking the type.

teaching_sequence.rationale: A reason has to be committed while both values are hidden, or the duel becomes arithmetic and the student learns to evaluate rather than to compare

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: With the same base, the larger exponent gives the larger value
With the same exponent, the larger base gives the larger value
With neither shared, one card must be rewritten before anything follows
A bigger base alone decides nothing: 2 to the power 10 is larger than 10 cubed

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read both cards out of the question text (each as a base and an exponent, or as a coefficient and a power of ten). Deal them without revealing either value. Read the valid reason tags from the item when it supplies them, otherwise compute them from whether the bases match, the exponents match or a rewrite exists.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.
question_integration.learn_source: props.learnQuestions (delivery_mode = 'Learn'). Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.
scene_fields: cardA and cardB, the two powers dealt
validReasons, the tags that genuinely settle this pair
valuesRevealed, always false until the reason is in
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no pair in it ('why is a bigger base not enough to decide?') has nothing to deal. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool 2 to the 10 against 10 to the 3 with both values revealed at 1024 and 1000, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.
question_integration.practice_source: props.questions (delivery_mode = 'Practice'), drawn at random by the platform inside the difficulty and subtype targets. Mandatory checkpoints are never served here.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the bigger-base reading fail on a pair the class would bet on. 2 to the power 10 is 1024 and 10 to the power 3 is 1000 - twenty four apart, so it cannot be dismissed as a freak big case. Ask for the guess OUT LOUD before you narrate the beat; the screen already carries the answer, and the value of the beat is that the class hears itself commit to the wrong rule first.

Beat 2 is the mechanism. 4 is 2 squared, so 4 to the power 4 becomes 2 to the power 2 all raised to the power 4, and the exponents multiply to 8. Both cards then read the SAME glyphs before either value appears - the class sees sameness rather than being told it, which is what settles the 'a duel must have a winner' objection.

Beat 3 is the edge that keeps the method honest. Neither 3 nor 5 is a whole number power of the other and the exponents 5 and 3 share no factor, so no rewrite exists - and the duel is STILL settled, at 243 against 125. Saying 'there is no shortcut here' is the method, not a failure, and it is also the answer to the opposite over-correction that a pair sharing nothing cannot be compared at all.
media.generation_prompt: Power Comparison Duel: two power cards dealt face up where the student picks the larger and then must supply the reason, and the values are not revealed until the reason is committed
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read both cards, their bases and their exponents. 2. Tap the card you think is larger before either value is shown. 3. Choose the reason your pick rests on. 4. Watch the reason applied, and read the rewritten card. 5. Reveal both values and check them against your reason. 6. Deal a new pair and try a reason you have not used yet. 7. Find a pair where no rewrite exists and say what has to be done instead. 8. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: How can every digit be written with a power of ten?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A place chart splits five thousand six hundred forty two into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, and each place becomes a digit times a power of ten. The chart then runs past the point, where tenths, hundredths and thousandths take negative exponents. Keeko doubts that the nine in the decimal is nine times ten to the power one.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: every place is a power of ten, and the places after the decimal point use negative exponents. Watch for students who give the tenths place the exponent one.

media.title: How can a very long number be written without miscounting zeroes?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The book's big facts, such as the Sun's distance from the centre of the galaxy, have so many zeroes that we may miscount them. The point is moved to leave one digit in front, and the number of places moved becomes the power of ten. Keeko doubts that fifty nine times ten squared is also scientific notation.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: scientific notation keeps a number from one up to ten in front and lets the power of ten count the places. Watch for students who leave two digits in front and still call it scientific notation.

video_script.why: Very long numbers are hard to read. Moving the point to leave one digit in front makes the power of ten do the counting.

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 12): The worldwide population of sheep (2024) is about 10 to the power 9, and that of goats is also about the same. What is the total population of sheep and goats? (i) 20 to the power 9 (ii) 10 to the power 11 (iii) 10 to the power 10 (iv) 10 to the power 18 (v) 2 × 10 to the power 9 (vi) 10 to the power 9 + 10 to the power 9
1. Adding two equal amounts doubles: 1 billion and 1 billion make 2 billion.
2. 10 to the power 9 + 10 to the power 9 is 2 × 10 to the power 9, so (v) and (vi) are the same number.
3. 20 to the power 9, 10 to the power 10, 10 to the power 11 and 10 to the power 18 multiply instead of adding, and are far too large.
4. The book lists only (vi), but (v) is equally correct.
Answer: (v) 2 × 10 to the power 9, which is the same as (vi)

content.text:
Tremendous in Ten! (game): In a game, each player has 10 seconds to write the larger number. Roxie wrote 10000000000000 and Estu wrote 999999 × 999999. Whose number is greater? In Round 2, Roxie wrote 10 to the power 1000 four times added, and Estu wrote 10 to the power 1000000 × 9000. Whose is greater?
1. Roxie's number is 1 followed by 13 zeroes, which is 10 to the power 13.
2. Estu's 999999 is less than 10 to the power 6, so his product is less than (10 to the power 6)², which is 10 to the power 12.
3. So Roxie wins Round 1.
4. Round 2: four copies of 10 to the power 1000 is 4 × 10 to the power 1000, while Estu's number has exponent 1000000, so Estu's is far greater.
Answer: Round 1: Roxie's number; Round 2: Estu's number

concepts.concept_name: Tulabhara: worth of an offering

content.text:
2.5 Did You Ever Wonder?
Nanjundappa wants to donate jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight. He is wondering how much it would cost.
Worth of jaggery (in rupees) = Roxie's weight in kg × cost of 1 kg jaggery. Worth of wheat (in rupees) = Estu's weight in kg × cost of 1 kg wheat.
Assuming Roxie's weight to be 45 kg and the cost of 1 kg of jaggery to be 70 rupees, the worth of donated jaggery is 45 × 70 = 3150 rupees.
Assuming Estu's weight to be 50 kg and the cost of 1 kg of wheat to be 50 rupees, the worth of donated wheat is 50 × 50 = 2500 rupees.
The practice of offering goods equal to the weight of a person, called Tulabhara or Tulabharam, is quite old and is still followed in many places in Southern India.

concepts.concept_name: Coins equal to a weight

content.text:
Roxie wonders, "Instead of jaggery if we use 1-rupee coins, how many coins are needed to equal my weight?"
1. Guessing: Make an instinctive guess of what the answer could be, without any calculations.
2. Calculating using estimation and approximation: (i) Describe the relationships among the quantities. (ii) Make reasonable assumptions and approximations. (iii) Compute and find the answer (and check how close your guess was).
Would the number of coins be in hundreds, thousands, lakhs, crores, or even more?

concepts.concept_name: Long walks: padayatra and walking around the Earth

content.text:
Estu says, "When I become an adult, I would like to donate notebooks worth my weight every year". Roxie says, "When I grow up, I would like to do annadana worth my weight every year". How many people might benefit from each of these offerings in a year?
Roxie and Estu overheard someone saying: "We did padayatra for about 400 km to reach this place! We arrived early this morning." How long ago would they have started their journey?
How many times can a person circumnavigate the Earth in their lifetime if they walk non-stop? Consider the distance around the Earth as 40000 km.

content.text:
1. Predict first: could one person walk around the Earth once in a lifetime, ten times, or a hundred times?
2. Assume a walking pace of about 5 km an hour and a life of about 70 years of non-stop walking.
3. Distance walked is 5 × 24 × 365 × 70 km, which is 3066000 km.
4. Divide by 40000 km: about 76 times around the Earth.

content.text:
Worked example: A group walked about 400 km. If they walked about 25 km a day, how long ago did they start? How many times could a person walk around the 40000 km Earth in 70 years of non-stop walking at 5 km an hour?
1. Padayatra: 400 ÷ 25 = 16, so they started about 16 days ago.
2. Distance in a lifetime: 5 km an hour for 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, for 70 years.
3. 5 × 24 × 365 × 70 = 3066000 km.
4. 3066000 ÷ 40000 ≈ 76.65, so about 76 times around the Earth.
Answer: About 16 days ago; about 76 times around the Earth

concepts.concept_name: Linear growth versus exponential growth

content.text:
Linear Growth vs. Exponential Growth
Roxie tells Estu about a science-fiction novel where they build a ladder to reach the moon: "I wonder if we actually had a ladder like that, how many steps would it have?"
Let's assume a reasonable distance of 20 cm. We have to find out how many 20 cm make 384400 km.
If we calculate the value, we get the result as 1922000000 steps, which is 192 crore and 20 lakh steps. The fixed increase in the distance with each step is called linear growth.
To cover the distance between the Earth and the Moon, it takes 1922000000 steps with linear growth whereas it takes just 46 folds of a piece of paper with exponential growth! Linear growth is additive, whereas exponential growth is multiplicative.
Can you come up with some examples of linear growth and of exponential growth?

content.text:
1. Predict first: would a ladder to the Moon have thousands, lakhs, crores or more steps?
2. Each step adds the same 20 cm, so the number of steps is distance divided by 20 cm.
3. 384400 km is 38440000000 cm, and dividing by 20 gives 1922000000 steps.
4. Folding multiplies by 2 each time and needs only 46 folds: multiplying beats adding.

content.text:
Worked example: How many 20 cm steps would a ladder to the Moon, 384400 km away, have? Compare it with folding paper.
1. 384400 km is 38440000000 cm, since 1 km is 100000 cm.
2. Steps: 38440000000 ÷ 20 = 1922000000, which is 192 crore 20 lakh steps.
3. Each step adds 20 cm: linear, additive growth.
4. Each fold doubles: 46 folds reach the Moon, exponential, multiplicative growth.
Answer: 1922000000 steps, about 192 crore, against just 46 folds

content.text:
Guess first, then write how the quantities are related.
A fixed amount added each day is linear growth.
content.publication_text:

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 2): There are 5 bottles in a container. Every day, a new container is brought in. How many bottles would there be after 40 days?
1. Each day adds one container of 5 bottles: the same amount added each day, linear growth.
2. After 40 days: 5 × 40 = 200 bottles.
3. In scientific notation 200 is 2 × 10².
Answer: 200 bottles, which is 2 × 10²

media.description: Jaggery equal to the weight of one child and wheat equal to the weight of another are to be donated. We assume sensible weights and prices for one kilogram, then multiply to estimate the worth of each. Keeko doubts that the worth is the weight plus the cost.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the worth of goods is the weight in kilograms times the cost of one kilogram. Watch for students who add the weight and the cost instead of multiplying.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How much is jaggery equal to a child's weight worth?
items: Estimate the worth of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight
source_video_walkthrough.intent: To estimate a worth we describe how the quantities relate, assume sensible values for the unknowns, and then multiply the weight by the cost of one kilogram.

interaction_points.prompt: What would the jaggery and the wheat be worth in rupees?
interaction_points.answer: About 3150 rupees of jaggery and about 2500 rupees of wheat
covers: Estimate the worth of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight

source: Estimate the worth of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight
video_script.why: To estimate a worth we describe how the quantities relate, assume sensible values for the unknowns, and then multiply the weight by the cost of one kilogram.
video_script.substitution: Write worth as weight in kilograms times the cost of one kilogram, put in sensible assumed values, and multiply.
video_script.anchor: jaggery and wheat equal to the weight of a child
video_script.wrong_answer: the worth is the weight plus the cost
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds 45 and 70 to get 115. But 70 rupees pays for only one kilogram, so 45 kilograms cost 70 rupees forty five times; we multiply.
video_script.payoff_line: The worth is the weight times the cost of one kilogram

final_answer.value: About 3150 rupees of jaggery and about 2500 rupees of wheat
final_answer.spoken: The jaggery is worth about three thousand one hundred fifty rupees. The wheat is worth about two thousand five hundred rupees.

names.Ruhee: the thirteen year old whose weight sets the jaggery
names.Jia: the person who plans to donate jaggery and wheat

maths_rules: worth of jaggery = weight in kg × cost of 1 kg of jaggery
assume 45 kg and 70 rupees for 1 kg: 45 × 70 = 3150
worth of wheat = weight in kg × cost of 1 kg of wheat
assume 50 kg and 50 rupees for 1 kg: 50 × 50 = 2500
the slip: 45 + 70 = 115 adds a weight to a price, which makes no sense
video_script.design: The two donations sit side by side. Each has a small line showing weight and the cost of one kilogram, then the multiplication is built beneath it.
open_questions: The weights 45 kg and 50 kg and the prices 70 and 50 rupees are the book's own assumptions.

media.title: How many one rupee coins weigh as much as a child?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Instead of jaggery, one rupee coins are used to equal the weight of a child. We assume the weights, change both to grams, and divide to estimate the number of coins. Keeko doubts dividing kilograms by grams directly.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: to find how many small things make up a big weight, put both weights in the same unit and divide. Watch for students who divide kilograms by grams directly.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many one rupee coins weigh as much as a child?
items: About how many 1-rupee coins weigh as much as Roxie
source_video_walkthrough.intent: A count of small things is the big weight divided by the small weight, with both in the same unit.

interaction_points.prompt: Would it be hundreds, thousands or lakhs?
interaction_points.answer: About 11250 coins, roughly 11 thousand
covers: About how many 1-rupee coins weigh as much as Roxie

source: About how many 1-rupee coins weigh as much as Roxie
video_script.why: A count of small things is the big weight divided by the small weight, with both in the same unit.
video_script.substitution: Change the child's weight to grams, then divide it by the weight of one coin.
video_script.anchor: one rupee coins that weigh as much as a child
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko divides 45 kg by 4 g and gets about 11. Kilograms and grams are different units; 45 kg is 45000 g, and 45000 divided by 4 is far larger.
video_script.payoff_line: Make both weights the same unit, then divide

final_answer.value: About 11250 coins, roughly 11 thousand
final_answer.spoken: About eleven thousand two hundred fifty coins are needed. That is roughly eleven thousand coins.

names.Ruhee: the child whose weight the one rupee coins must equal

maths_rules: number of coins = weight of the child ÷ weight of one coin
assume 45 kg and a coin of about 4 g
the slip: 45 ÷ 4 mixes kg with g
video_script.design: A balance carries the child on one pan and coins on the other. The two weights are written in the same unit before the division is built.
open_questions: The coin weight of about 4 g is the worklist's assumption; the book suggests measuring a coin.

media.title: How long ago did the group start, and how far could a person walk?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A group walked about four hundred kilometres to reach a place. We assume how far they walk in a day to find when they started, then assume a lifetime of non-stop walking to count the rounds of the Earth. Keeko doubts a daily distance that leaves out the hours.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: state each assumption, then multiply the rates one step at a time. Watch for students who use the distance for one hour as if it were the distance for a whole day.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How long ago did the group start, and how far could a person walk?
items: A group walked about 400 km; how many times can a person walk around the Earth in a lifetime
source_video_walkthrough.intent: Questions without all the numbers are solved by stating sensible assumptions and then combining the rates one step at a time.

interaction_points.prompt: Then, how many times could a person walk around the Earth in a lifetime?
interaction_points.answer: About 16 days ago; about 76 times around the Earth
covers: A group walked about 400 km; how many times can a person walk around the Earth in a lifetime

source: A group walked about 400 km; how many times can a person walk around the Earth in a lifetime
video_script.why: Questions without all the numbers are solved by stating sensible assumptions and then combining the rates one step at a time.
video_script.substitution: Assume a distance for one hour or one day, then multiply or divide in single steps.
video_script.anchor: a long walk of about 400 km, and a lifetime of walking round the Earth
video_script.wrong_answer: about three times around the Earth
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko uses 5 km for a whole day, so 5 × 365 × 70 = 127750 km, about 3 times around. But 5 km is the distance for one hour; a day has 24 hours, so a day gives 5 × 24 = 120 km.
video_script.payoff_line: State each assumption, then multiply the rates one step at a time

final_answer.value: About 16 days ago; about 76 times around the Earth
final_answer.spoken: The group started about sixteen days ago. A person could walk around the Earth about seventy six times.

names.Laksh: one of the two children who overhear the group
names.Ruhee: one of the two children who overhear the group

maths_rules: assume the group walked 25 km in a day: 400 ÷ 25 = 16 days
assume 5 km in each hour, non-stop: 5 × 24 = 120 km a day
the distance around the Earth is 40000 km: 3066000 ÷ 40000 = 76.65, so about 76 full times
the slip: 5 × 365 × 70 = 127750 km, about 3 times, leaves out the 24 hours
video_script.design: A long road line carries the walk. The walking rates are written in a chain on the working area, each step building on the one before.
open_questions: The 25 km a day, 5 km an hour and 70 years are assumptions taken from the worklist; the book leaves them to the learner.

media.title: How many steps would a ladder to the Moon have?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A ladder to the Moon has steps twenty centimetres apart, and the Moon is 384400 kilometres away. We change kilometres to centimetres and divide to count the steps. The result is compared with folding paper, where each fold doubles the thickness.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: put both lengths in the same unit before dividing to count steps. Watch for students who divide kilometres by centimetres directly.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many steps would a ladder to the Moon have?
items: How many 20 cm steps would a ladder to the Moon, 384400 km away, have?
source_video_walkthrough.intent: To count equal steps in a long distance, both lengths must be in the same unit; the same fixed gain at every step is linear growth, unlike doubling.

interaction_points.prompt: If each step rises twenty centimetres, how many steps are needed?
interaction_points.answer: 1922000000 steps, about 192 crore, against just 46 folds
covers: How many 20 cm steps would a ladder to the Moon, 384400 km away, have?

source: How many 20 cm steps would a ladder to the Moon, 384400 km away, have?
video_script.why: To count equal steps in a long distance, both lengths must be in the same unit; the same fixed gain at every step is linear growth, unlike doubling.
video_script.substitution: Change kilometres to centimetres, then divide the distance by the height of one step.
video_script.anchor: a ladder to the Moon with steps of 20 cm, against folding paper
video_script.wrong_answer: nineteen thousand two hundred twenty steps
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko divides 384400 km by 20 cm as plain numbers and gets 19220 steps. The units differ: 384400 km is 38440000000 cm, so the true count is 1922000000.
video_script.payoff_line: Put both lengths in the same unit, then divide to count the steps

final_answer.value: 1922000000 steps, about 192 crore, against just 46 folds
final_answer.spoken: The ladder needs about one hundred ninety two crore steps. Folding paper takes only forty six folds.

names.Ruhee: the child who reads about a ladder to the Moon in a novel

maths_rules: linear growth adds the same amount each time; exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each time
the slip: 384400 ÷ 20 = 19220 mixes km with cm
video_script.design: A tall ladder rises from the Earth towards the Moon, with a few steps labelled 20 cm. The conversion and division are built on the working area, and the paper folds appear at the end for comparison.

concepts.concept_name: Populations as powers of 10

content.text:
Getting a Sense for Large Numbers
A lakh is 10 to the power 5 (100000), a crore is 10 to the power 7 (10000000), and an arab is 10 to the power 9, whereas a million is 10 to the power 6 and a billion is 10 to the power 9.
As of mid-2025, there are only two northern white rhinos remaining in the world. There are just 242 Kakapo alive. As of 2018, there are around 4.15 lakh African elephants.
The estimated global population of starlings is around 1.3 arab or 1.3 billion. The global human population as of 2025 is 8.2 arab or 8.2 billion.
The estimated mosquito population worldwide (2023) is 11 neel or 110 trillion.
With a global human population of about 8 × 10 to the power 9 and about 4 × 10 to the power 5 African elephants, can we say that there are nearly 20000 people for every African elephant?

1. Predict first: are there more starlings or more people in the world?
2. 1.3 billion starlings is 1.3 × 10 to the power 9; people are 8.2 × 10 to the power 9, so more people.

4. People per elephant: 8 ÷ 4 is 2, and 9 − 5 is 4, so 2 × 10⁴, which is 20000.

content.text:
Worked example: Write the starling and mosquito populations in scientific notation, and check that there are about 20000 people for every African elephant.
1. 1.3 billion is 1300000000, which is 1.3 × 10 to the power 9 starlings.
2. 110 trillion is 110000000000000, which is 1.1 × 10 to the power 14 mosquitoes.
3. People per elephant: 8 × 10 to the power 9 divided by 4 × 10 to the power 5.
4. Divide the coefficients, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, and subtract the exponents, 9 − 5 = 4: 2 × 10⁴ = 20000.
Answer: 1.3 × 10 to the power 9 starlings, 1.1 × 10 to the power 14 mosquitoes, and yes, about 20000 people per elephant

concepts.concept_name: Calculating with numbers in scientific notation

content.text:
The estimated population of ants globally is 20 padma or 20 quadrillion (2 × 10 to the power 16).
The estimated number of trees (2023) globally stands at 3 trillion (3 × 10 to the power 12).
Calculate and write the answer using scientific notation: (i) How many ants are there for every human in the world? (ii) If a flock of starlings contains 10000 birds, how many flocks could there be in the world? (iii) If each tree had about 10⁴ leaves, find the total number of leaves on all the trees in the world. (iv) If you stacked sheets of paper on top of each other, how many would you need to reach the Moon?

content.text:
Worked example: Find, in scientific notation, the ants per human, the flocks of 10000 starlings, the leaves on all trees, and the sheets of paper (0.001 cm thick) needed to reach the Moon 384400 km away.
1. Ants per human: 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 and 16 − 9 = 7, so 0.25 × 10 to the power 7, which is 2.5 × 10 to the power 6.
2. Flocks: 1.3 × 10 to the power 9 divided by 10⁴ is 1.3 × 10 to the power 5.
3. Leaves: 3 × 10 to the power 12 times 10⁴ is 3 × 10 to the power 16.
4. Sheets: 384400 km is 3.844 × 10 to the power 10 cm, and each sheet is 10 to the power −3 cm, so 3.844 × 10 to the power 13 sheets.
Answer: 2.5 × 10 to the power 6 ants per human, 1.3 × 10 to the power 5 flocks, 3 × 10 to the power 16 leaves, 3.844 × 10 to the power 13 sheets

content.text:
A different way to say your age!
"I'm 4840 days old today!" said Roxie. "I'm ______ hours old!" said Roxie. Make an estimate before finding this number.
Roxie says, "I am 6970710 ... old". What could this number mean? Find out!
Estu: "I am 4070 days old today. Can you find out my date of birth?"
If you have lived for a million seconds, how old would you be?

content.text:
1. Predict first: is a million seconds a few days, a few months or a few years?
2. Hours: 4840 days × 24 hours a day is 116160 hours.
3. 6970710 is too big for hours; in minutes, 4840 days is 4840 × 24 × 60, about 6969600, so it is minutes.
4. A day has 86400 seconds, so a million seconds is about 11.57 days, less than two weeks.

content.text:
Worked example: Roxie is 4840 days old. Find her age in hours, decide what unit 6970710 is in, find Estu's age in years for 4070 days, and find how many days a million seconds is.
1. Hours: 4840 × 24 = 116160 hours.
2. Minutes: 6970710 ÷ 1440 is about 4840.8 days, so 6970710 is Roxie's age in minutes.
3. Estu: 4070 ÷ 365 is 11 with 55 days left; allowing about 3 leap days, he is 11 years and about 52 days old, so count back that far from today.
4. A day has 24 × 60 × 60 = 86400 seconds, and 1000000 ÷ 86400 ≈ 11.57 days.
Answer: 116160 hours; 6970710 minutes; Estu is about 11 years and 52 days old; a million seconds is about 11.6 days

concepts.concept_name: A time scale in powers of 10 seconds

content.text:
Time in seconds, compared to real-world events: 10 to the power 0 seconds, time taken for a ball thrown up to fall back; 10 to the power 1 seconds, time blood takes to complete one circulation; about 10² seconds, making a cup of tea.
10 to the power 5 seconds is about 1.16 days and 10 to the power 6 seconds is about 11.57 days.
Notice how rapid exponential growth is: 10 to the power 6 seconds is less than a fortnight, but 10 to the power 9 seconds is a whopping 31 years.
A fossil of a terror bird is dated to 15 million years ago. Plants on land started 47 crore years ago.
Calculate and write the answer using scientific notation: (i) If one star is counted every second, how long would it take to count all the stars in the universe? (ii) If one could drink a glass of water (200 ml) every 10 seconds, how long would it take to finish the entire volume of water on Earth?

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 10 to the power 9 seconds closer to a month, a year or a lifetime?
2. A year is about 3.15 × 10 to the power 7 seconds, so multiply years by that.
3. 15 million years is about 4.7 × 10 to the power 14 seconds; 47 crore years is about 1.5 × 10 to the power 16 seconds.
4. Each step up the scale multiplies by 10, so a few steps take us from days to lifetimes.

content.text:
Worked example: Convert 15 million years to seconds. How long would it take to count 2 × 10 to the power 23 stars at one per second, and to drink 2 × 10 to the power 25 drops of water (16 drops per ml) at 200 ml every 10 seconds?
1. One year is about 3.15 × 10 to the power 7 seconds.
2. 15 million years: 1.5 × 10 to the power 7 years times 3.15 × 10 to the power 7 s, about 4.7 × 10 to the power 14 seconds.
3. Stars: one per second, so 2 × 10 to the power 23 seconds.
4. Water: 2 × 10 to the power 25 drops is 1.25 × 10 to the power 24 ml, which is 6.25 × 10 to the power 21 glasses; at 10 seconds a glass that is 6.25 × 10 to the power 22 seconds.

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 13): Calculate and write the answer in scientific notation: (i) If each person in the world had 30 pieces of clothing, find the total number of pieces of clothing. (ii) There are about 100 million bee colonies in the world. Find the number of honeybees if each colony has about 50000 bees. (iii) The human body has about 38 trillion bacterial cells. Find the bacterial population residing in all humans in the world. (iv) Total time spent eating in a lifetime in seconds.
1. (i) 8.2 × 10 to the power 9 people times 30 is 246 × 10 to the power 9, which is 2.46 × 10 to the power 11.
2. (ii) 10 to the power 8 colonies times 5 × 10⁴ bees is 5 × 10 to the power 12.
3. (iii) 3.8 × 10 to the power 13 cells times 8.2 × 10 to the power 9 people is 31.16 × 10 to the power 22, which is 3.116 × 10 to the power 23.
4. (iv) Assume 1 hour of eating a day for 70 years: 3600 × 365 × 70 = 91980000 seconds, which is 9.198 × 10 to the power 7.
Answer: (i) 2.46 × 10 to the power 11 (ii) 5 × 10 to the power 12 (iii) 3.116 × 10 to the power 23 (iv) about 9.198 × 10 to the power 7 seconds

tool_config.title: Standard Form Fixer
tool_config.idea: A product or quotient in scientific notation is found by multiplying or dividing the coefficients and combining the exponents of 10, and then the answer is put in standard form by sliding the decimal point until the coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10 and changing the exponent to match.
tool_config.screen: Two numbers in scientific notation, each as a coefficient block and a power of 10 block, and a result card with a decimal point that can be slid left or right. An exponent counter moves the opposite way as the point slides.
student_does: Read the coefficient and the exponent of each number.
Predict the result before standard form is reached.
Combine the coefficients and the exponents on the result card.
Slide the decimal point until the coefficient is between 1 and 10 and read the new exponent.
challenges: (2 × 10 to the power 16) ÷ (8 × 10 to the power 9): write the answer in standard form.
(4 × 10 to the power 6) × (5 × 10 to the power 3): write the answer in standard form.
(6 × 10 to the power 8) ÷ (2 × 10 to the power 3): write the answer in standard form.
(7 × 10 to the power 4) × (9 × 10 to the power 5): write the answer in standard form.
(2 × 10 to the power 5) ÷ (8 × 10 to the power 9): write the answer in standard form.
(1.5 × 10 to the power 7) × (3.15 × 10 to the power 7): write the answer in standard form.
feedback: A coefficient left outside 1 to 10 is marked as not yet in standard form.
Sliding the point one place left shows the exponent going up by one, and one place right shows it going down.
A result judged by its coefficient alone is tested against the exponents and shown to fail.
tool_config.done_when: All six cards are done with the coefficient between 1 and 10 and the exponent matching.

source_video_walkthrough.intent: A huge count is clearer as one digit before the point times a power of ten, and the power comes from counting the hops of the point.

interaction_points.prompt: Think and tell.

video_script.why: A huge count is clearer as one digit before the point times a power of ten, and the power comes from counting the hops of the point.
video_script.substitution: Write the number in full, count the hops of the point to sit after the first digit, and use the count as the power of ten.

video_script.wrong_answer: one point one times ten to the power thirteen

video_script.payoff_line: The hops of the point give the power of ten, and dividing subtracts the powers

media.title: How do we change an age from days into other units?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: One child is 4840 days old, another is 4070 days old, and a number with no unit might be an age. We change days into hours and minutes, days into years and days, and a million seconds into days. Keeko doubts the unit chosen for the large number.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a smaller unit gives a bigger count, so estimate before deciding the unit. Watch for students who pick the unit for a large number without testing it.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do we change an age from days into other units?
items: Roxie is 4840 days old: find the age in hours, decide the unit of 6970710, find Estu's age in years for 4070 days, and a million seconds in days
source_video_walkthrough.intent: Time units are changed by multiplying or dividing by how many small units make one big unit, and a smaller unit gives a bigger count.
source_video_walkthrough.withheld: 116160 hours; 6970710 minutes; 11 years and 52 days; 11.6 days

interaction_points.prompt: And how many days is a million seconds?
interaction_points.answer: 116160 hours; 6970710 minutes; about 11 years and 52 days old; about 11.6 days
covers: Roxie is 4840 days old: find the age in hours, decide the unit of 6970710, find Estu's age in years for 4070 days, and a million seconds in days

source: Roxie is 4840 days old: find the age in hours, decide the unit of 6970710, find Estu's age in years for 4070 days, and a million seconds in days
video_script.why: Time units are changed by multiplying or dividing by how many small units make one big unit, and a smaller unit gives a bigger count.
video_script.substitution: Multiply to go to a smaller unit and divide to go to a bigger one, then test a large number against the age in days.
video_script.anchor: ages in days, a number with no unit, and a million seconds
video_script.wrong_answer: the number is the age in seconds
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees that 6970710 is large and says it must be seconds. But 4840 days is 4840 × 86400 = 418176000 seconds, far bigger; the number fits minutes, since 4840 × 1440 is about 6969600.
video_script.payoff_line: A smaller unit gives a bigger count, so estimate before you decide the unit

final_answer.value: 116160 hours; 6970710 minutes; about 11 years and 52 days old; about 11.6 days
final_answer.spoken: The first child is one hundred sixteen thousand one hundred sixty hours old. The other number is the age in minutes. The second child is about eleven years and fifty two days old. A million seconds is about eleven point six days.

maths_rules: 1 day = 24 × 60 = 1440 minutes: 4840 × 1440 = 6969600, close to 6970710, so the unit is minutes
in seconds the age would be 4840 × 86400 = 418176000, far bigger than 6970710
4070 days: 11 × 365 = 4015 and 4070 − 4015 = 55; about 3 leap days in 11 years give 55 − 3 = 52, so about 11 years and 52 days
video_script.design: A row of four small panels, one for each question, each showing a day and the unit it is changed into. The working area builds one conversion at a time.
open_questions: The 3 leap days in 11 years follow the worklist's 'about 52'; 4070 days is 11 years and 55 days without leap days.

media.title: How many seconds is fifteen million years?
media.context: Power Play. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Fifteen million years is changed into seconds using powers of ten. Then the time to count every star of the universe, and the time to drink all the drops of water on Earth, are found. Keeko doubts that only the unit changes.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: work on the numbers in front and the powers of ten separately, then put them together. Watch for students who change the unit but keep the same number, as if a year were one second.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many seconds is fifteen million years?
items: Convert 15 million years to seconds; time to count 2 × 10 to the power 23 stars at one per second; time to drink 2 × 10 to the power 25 drops at 200 ml every 10 seconds
source_video_walkthrough.intent: Huge times are found by working on the numbers in front and the powers of ten separately: multiply the numbers and add the powers, or divide the numbers and subtract the powers.

interaction_points.prompt: How long would it take?
interaction_points.answer: about 4.7 × 10 to the power 14 seconds; 2 × 10 to the power 23 seconds; 6.25 × 10 to the power 22 seconds
covers: Convert 15 million years to seconds; time to count 2 × 10 to the power 23 stars at one per second; time to drink 2 × 10 to the power 25 drops at 200 ml every 10 seconds

source: Convert 15 million years to seconds; time to count 2 × 10 to the power 23 stars at one per second; time to drink 2 × 10 to the power 25 drops at 200 ml every 10 seconds
video_script.why: Huge times are found by working on the numbers in front and the powers of ten separately: multiply the numbers and add the powers, or divide the numbers and subtract the powers.
video_script.substitution: Write each quantity with one digit before the point and a power of ten, then multiply or divide the numbers in front and add or subtract the powers.
video_script.anchor: fifteen million years in seconds, counting every star, and drinking every drop of water
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko changes only the unit and keeps the number, so fifteen million years becomes fifteen million seconds. But one year alone is about 3.15 × 10 to the power 7 seconds, so the seconds are about 4.7 × 10 to the power 14.

final_answer.value: about 4.7 × 10 to the power 14 seconds; 2 × 10 to the power 23 seconds; 6.25 × 10 to the power 22 seconds
final_answer.spoken: Fifteen million years is about four point seven times ten to the power fourteen seconds. Counting takes two times ten to the power twenty three seconds. Drinking takes six point two five times ten to the power twenty two seconds.

video_script.why: A product of big numbers is found by multiplying the numbers in front and adding the powers of ten, then moving the point so the front number lies between one and ten.

content.text:
Figure it Out (power play, question 14): What was the date 1 arab or 1 billion seconds ago?
1. A day has 86400 seconds.
2. 1000000000 ÷ 86400 ≈ 11574 days.
3. 11574 ÷ 365 is about 31.7 years.
4. Count back about 31 years and 8 months from today's date.
Answer: About 11574 days, or about 31.7 years, before today

concepts.concept_name: Indian names for powers of 10

content.text:
2.5 A Pinch of History
In the Lalitavistara, a Buddhist treatise from the first century BCE, we see number-names for odd powers of ten up to 10 to the power 53.
"Hundred kotis are called an ayuta (10 to the power 9), hundred ayutas a niyuta (10 to the power 11), hundred niyutas a kankara (10 to the power 13), ..., a hundred vibhutangamas is a tallakshana (10 to the power 53)."
Mahaviracharya gives a list of 24 terms in his treatise Ganita-sara-sangraha. An anonymous Jaina treatise Amalasiddhi gives a name for each power of ten up to 10 to the power 96. A Pali grammar treatise of Kaccayana lists number-names up to 10 to the power 140.
A hundred thousand is a lakh: 100 × 1000 = 100000, and 10² × 10³ is 10 to the power 5. A hundred lakhs is a crore. A hundred crores is an arab. A hundred arab is a kharab.
Continuing this, a hundred kharab is a neel, a hundred neel is a padma, a hundred padma is a shankh and a hundred shankh is a maha shankh.

content.text:
Worked example: Starting from a lakh as 10² × 10³, find the powers of 10 for a crore, an arab, a kharab and a neel.
1. A lakh is 100 × 1000 = 100000, which is 10 to the power 2 + 3, 10 to the power 5.
2. A crore is 100 lakh: 10² × 10 to the power 5 gives 10 to the power 7.
3. An arab is 100 crore: 10 to the power 9. A kharab is 100 arab: 10 to the power 11.
4. A neel is 100 kharab: 10 to the power 13.
Answer: Crore 10 to the power 7, arab 10 to the power 9, kharab 10 to the power 11, neel 10 to the power 13

concepts.concept_name: International names, googol and googolplex

content.text:
In the American or International system, we say: A thousand thousand is a million, 10³ × 10³ is 10 to the power 6. A thousand million is a billion, 10³ × 10 to the power 6 is 10 to the power 9. A thousand billion is a trillion, 10 to the power 12.
Continuing this, a thousand trillion is a quadrillion (10 to the power 15). Observe the names million, billion, trillion, quadrillion, quintillion, sextillion, septillion, octillion, nonillion, decillion.
The number 10 to the power 100 is also called a googol. The estimated number of atoms in the universe is 10 to the power 78 to 10 to the power 82. The number 10 to the power googol is called a googolplex.
The highest numerical value banknote ever printed was a special note valued 1 sextillion pengo (10 to the power 21) printed in Hungary in 1946. In 2009, Zimbabwe printed a 100 trillion (10 to the power 14) Zimbabwean dollar note.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the powers of 10 for a billion, a trillion and a quintillion, and compare a googol with the number of atoms in the universe.
1. A million is 1000 × 1000, which is 10 to the power 6.
2. A billion is a thousand million: 10 to the power 6 + 3, 10 to the power 9.
3. A trillion is 10 to the power 12, a quadrillion 10 to the power 15 and a quintillion 10 to the power 18.
4. A googol is 10 to the power 100; the atoms are at most 10 to the power 82, so a googol is 10 to the power 18 times as many.
Answer: Billion 10 to the power 9, trillion 10 to the power 12, quintillion 10 to the power 18; a googol is far larger

content.text:
A pinch of history: the names: Observe the names million (10 to the power 6), billion (10 to the power 9), trillion (10 to the power 12), quadrillion (10 to the power 15), quintillion (10 to the power 18). What does the first part of each name denote?
1. Write each as 1000 multiplied by more 1000s: a billion is 1000 × 1000 × 1000.
2. bi means 2: a billion is 1000 with 2 more 1000s multiplied, 10 to the power 3 + 3 × 2.
3. tri means 3: a trillion is 10 to the power 3 + 3 × 3, which is 10 to the power 12.
4. quadri means 4 and quinti means 5, giving 10 to the power 15 and 10 to the power 18.
Answer: The first part counts how many times 1000 is multiplied onto 1000: bi 2, tri 3, quadri 4, quinti 5

media.description: In the international system each name is a thousand times the one before. We find the powers of ten for a billion, a trillion and a quintillion, and compare a googol with the number of atoms in the universe. Keeko doubts how the powers combine.

video_script.why: Each international name is a thousand times the one before, and multiplying powers of ten adds the powers, so each name raises the power by three.

final_answer.value: Billion 10 to the power 9, trillion 10 to the power 12, quintillion 10 to the power 18; a googol is far larger

media.description: The names million, billion, trillion, quadrillion and quintillion are each a row of thousands multiplied together. We write each as thousands, count the extra thousands, and see what the first part of the name stands for.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the first part of the name counts the extra thousands multiplied onto the first thousand. Watch for students who read bi as ten to the power two instead of two extra thousands.

source_video_walkthrough.intent: Each international name adds three to the power of ten, so a name is a row of thousands, and the first part counts the thousands after the first.

interaction_points.prompt: What does it tell us?
interaction_points.answer: The first part counts how many times 1000 is multiplied onto 1000: bi 2, tri 3, quadri 4, quinti 5

video_script.why: Each international name adds three to the power of ten, so a name is a row of thousands, and the first part counts the thousands after the first.

video_script.anchor: the names million, billion, trillion, quadrillion and quintillion
video_script.payoff_line: The first part counts how many more thousands are multiplied onto the first thousand

final_answer.value: The first part counts how many times 1000 is multiplied onto 1000: bi 2, tri 3, quadri 4, quinti 5
final_answer.spoken: The first part counts how many more thousands are multiplied onto the first thousand. Bi is two, tri is three, quadri is four and quinti is five.

maths_rules: a million = 10⁶ = 10³ × 10³ = 1000 × 1000: the first 1000 and 1 more
a billion = 10⁹ = 10³ × 10³ × 10³: the first 1000 and 2 more, bi = 2
a trillion = 10¹² = 4 thousands: the first 1000 and 3 more, tri = 3
a quadrillion = 10¹⁵ = 5 thousands: the first 1000 and 4 more, quadri = 4
a quintillion = 10¹⁸ = 6 thousands: the first 1000 and 5 more, quinti = 5
check: the power = 3 + 3 × (the number): tri gives 3 + 9 = 12, quinti gives 3 + 15 = 18
video_script.design: Each name is drawn as a row of thousand blocks. The first block is plain and the extra blocks are coloured, and a counter under the extra blocks shows the number.

concepts.concept_name: What powers did in this chapter

content.text:
We analysed some situations, asked questions, and found answers by first guessing, then modelling the problem statement, followed by making assumptions and approximations to carry out the calculations.
We experienced how rapid exponential growth, also called multiplicative growth, can be compared to additive growth.
n to the power a is n × n × n × ... × n (n multiplied by itself a times), and n to the power −a is 1 over n to the power a.
Operations with exponents satisfy: n to the power a × n to the power b = n to the power a + b; (n to the power a) to the power b = n to the power a × b; n to the power a ÷ n to the power b = n to the power a − b; n to the power a × m to the power a = (n × m) to the power a; n to the power a ÷ m to the power a = (n ÷ m) to the power a; n to the power 0 is 1 (n ≠ 0).
The scientific notation for the number 308100000 is 3.081 × 10 to the power 8. The standard form of any number is x × 10 to the power y, where x ≥ 1 and x < 10, and y is an integer.
Engaging in interesting thought experiments can be used as means to understand how large a number or a quantity is.

content.text:
1. Our opening question is settled: 46 folds of a 0.001 cm sheet give about 7 lakh km, beyond the Moon.
2. A power counts factors; the rules for exponents come from counting factors and cancelling them.
3. Standard form puts the size of a number in its exponent of 10.
4. Still open for you: play Tremendous in Ten with a friend and find the largest number you can write.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students restate the meaning of a power, the exponent rules for products, quotients, powers of powers and zero and negative exponents, and the standard form for large numbers.

objectives.objective_text: Students start from a sheet 0.001 cm thick, double the thickness for each fold, and fill the thickness table up to 17 folds, where it is about 131 cm.
Students guess and then find the thickness after 26, 27 and 30 folds by doubling, and compare them with the 830 m Burj Khalifa and the 11 km deep Mariana Trench.
Students show that any two folds multiply the thickness by 4, any three folds by 8, and any ten folds by 1024, and explain why this is called multiplicative or exponential growth.
Students fill the thickness table from fold 21 to fold 46 by doubling, converting centimetres to metres and kilometres, and find the fold where the stack passes the Moon.
Students write the thickness after n folds as 0.001 × 2 to the power n, read powers aloud, and name the base and the exponent in 5 to the power 4, which is 625.
Students choose 2 to the power 10 times v as the thickness after 10 folds, reject the other expressions, and contrast 4 + 4 + 4, which is 12, with 4 × 4 × 4, which is 64.
Students find (−4) cubed, decide whether (−1) to the powers 5 and 56 are positive or negative, verify that (−2) to the power 4 is 16, and find powers of zero.
Students write a × a × a × b × b as a cubed b squared, and express 32400 in exponential form as a product of powers of its prime factors 2, 3 and 5.
Students write repeated products in exponential form, express numbers as products of powers of primes, and find the values of powers, including powers with negative bases.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students follow the king's 3 daughters, baskets, keys and rooms, find that there are 3 to the power 4 rooms and 3 to the power 7 diamonds, and compute both by repeated multiplication.
Students regroup seven 3s into two powers of the same base in two ways, multiply p to the power 4 by p to the power 6 by adding the exponents, and compute three powers.
Students evaluate 4 to the power 6 as the square of 4 cubed and as the cube of 4 squared, rewrite two more numbers as a power of a power, and state the rule.
Students write 8 to the power 6, 7 to the power 15, 9 to the power 14 and 5 to the power 8 as a power of a power in two different ways by splitting each exponent into two factors.
Students decide whether statements about squares, cubes and higher powers are always, sometimes or never true, and describe the numbers that are both squares and cubes as sixth powers.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students reason that a pond whose lotuses double every day and is full on day 30 was half covered on day 29, and write both counts in exponential form.
Students count Damayanti's lotuses after 4 days of doubling and 4 days of tripling, show that the order does not change the count, and multiply powers with the same exponent by multiplying the bases.
Students simplify 10 to the power 4 divided by 5 to the power 4 by pairing each 10 with a 5, getting 2 to the power 4, which is 16, and state the rule for dividing powers with equal exponents.
Students rewrite products of powers on the prime bases 2 and 3 to decide which of five numbers written with exponents are the same number.
Students count Estu's dress and cap combinations as 4 × 3, which is 12, using a tree of choices, and extend the idea to Roxie's dresses, hats and shoes.
Students count passwords for a 2-digit and a 3-digit lock by solving simpler locks first, and show that a 5-digit lock has 10 to the power 5 passwords.
Students count the passwords of a lock with 6 slots of letters A to Z as 26 to the power 6, and look at how pincodes, mobile numbers and vehicle numbers are built from slots.
Students count alphanumeric passcodes of length 5 as 36 to the power 5 and find how many digits a code needs to give 8.5 billion milk packets each a different code.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students use halving on a line of 16 units once, twice and three times, and write each length as a power of 2 as they cancel and divide out factors of 2.

Students generalise the halving pattern: to divide powers of the same base, subtract the exponents. They use it for 2 to the power 100 divided by 2 to the power 25 and explain why the base cannot be 0.
Students rewrite 4 to the power 32 as a power of 2, divide 2 to the power 224 by it by subtracting exponents, and find the units digit from the cycle of units digits of powers of 2.
Students define 2 to the power 0 so that the division rule still works, showing that 2⁴ divided by 2⁴ is 1, and generalise that x to the power 0 is 1 for any nonzero x.
Students continue halving a 16-unit line 5 times and 10 times, get half a unit and one sixty-fourth of a unit, and write these lengths with negative exponents as powers of 2.
Students write 10 to the power −3 and 7 to the power −2 as fractions, show that 10 cubed is 1 over 10 to the power −3, and check that the exponent rules also hold for integer exponents.
Students write 2 to the power −4, 10 to the power −5, (−7) to the power −2, (−5) to the power −3 and 10 to the power −100 as one over a positive power.
Students simplify products of powers that have negative exponents by adding the exponents, including 2⁴ × (−4) to the power −2 and 8 to the power p times 8 to the power q.
Students simplify products, quotients and powers of powers with negative exponents into exponential form, and write one number as a product of powers in three different ways.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students arrange the powers of 4 from 4 to the power −2 up to 4 to the power 8 on a line and compute products and quotients such as 65536 divided by 64 by moving along the line.
Students show that 16384 is 16 times larger than 1024 by dividing two powers of 4, and find how many times larger 4 squared is than 4 to the power −2.
Students build the power line of 7 from 7 to the power −4 to 7 to the power 7 and write products and quotients of its numbers as single powers of 7.
Students write 47561, 172, 5642 and 6374 in expanded form using powers of 10, and write the decimal 561.903 using negative powers of 10 for the decimal places.
Students write 5900 as a number from 1 up to 10 times a power of 10, and write three very large facts about the Sun, the galaxy and the Earth in scientific notation.
Students compare changing the coefficient and changing the exponent in Mumbai's population, and use Kohima's population to explain that the digits of the coefficient show how precise a number is.

Students compare the Sun to Saturn, Saturn to Uranus and Sun to Earth distances written in standard form, find the smallest by comparing exponents first, and mark the Earth's relative position on a number line.
Students write 59853, 65950, 3430000 and 70040000000 in standard form by moving the decimal point and counting the places moved.
Students decide the greater of two powers with a reason, scale a given square to decimals and larger numbers, and choose the correct total of two populations of about 10 to the power 9.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students write the worth of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight as weight times cost per kilogram, assume weights and prices, and compute 45 × 70 and 50 × 50 rupees.
Students guess and then estimate how many 1-rupee coins balance Roxie's weight by assuming the weight of a coin, and extend it to 5-rupee coins and 10-rupee notes.
Students estimate how long a 400 km padayatra took and how many times a person could walk around the 40000 km Earth in a lifetime, stating each assumption about walking speed and time.
Students count the 20 cm steps of a ladder to the Moon, about 192 crore steps, compare it with 46 folds of paper, and give examples of additive and multiplicative growth.
Students model a container problem as repeated addition, compute the total after 40 days, and write the answer in scientific notation.
Students connect lakh, crore and arab to powers of 10, write animal populations such as starlings and mosquitoes in scientific notation, and estimate the number of people for every African elephant.

Students find ants per human, flocks of starlings, leaves on all trees and sheets of paper to the Moon, calculating in scientific notation: they multiply or divide the coefficients and combine the exponents.
Students turn Roxie's 4840 days into hours, decide what her 6970710 means, find Estu's birthday from 4070 days, and work out how old someone is after a million seconds.
Students place events from a falling ball to the age of the Earth on a time scale of powers of 10 seconds, convert two ancient ages to seconds, and estimate two very long times.
Students estimate totals such as clothes, honeybees, bacteria and eating time in scientific notation, and find the date one billion seconds ago.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.

Students build million, billion and trillion by multiplying by 1000, so each exponent grows by 3, and meet the googol, 10 to the power 100, the googolplex, and record banknotes.
Students work out what the first part of each international number name denotes by writing each name as a power of 1000 times 1000.
Students restate the meaning of a power, the exponent rules for products, quotients, powers of powers and zero and negative exponents, and the standard form for large numbers.
